```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

# Same simulated nitrate population and sample as the lab
beta_0 <- 4
beta_1 <- 0.035
sigma <- 2

ag_pct <- runif(1e4, 0, 80)
nitrate_hat <- beta_0 + beta_1 * ag_pct
nitrate <- rnorm(1e4, nitrate_hat, sigma)
simulated_population <- tibble(ag_pct, nitrate_hat, nitrate)

one_sample <- slice_sample(simulated_population, n = 30)
one_sample_lm <- lm(nitrate ~ ag_pct, one_sample)
beta_1_hat <- coef(one_sample_lm)[["ag_pct"]]
se_beta_1 <- coef(summary(one_sample_lm))["ag_pct", "Std. Error"]

# Least squares slope, without the overhead of lm()
ols_slope <- function(x, y) cov(x, y) / var(x)

# Scatter plot of nitrate by farmland with its least squares line
plot_wells <- function(wells, line_colour = "firebrick", alpha = 0.6) {
  slope <- ols_slope(wells$ag_pct, wells$nitrate)
  ggplot(wells, aes(ag_pct, nitrate)) +
    geom_point(
      shape = 21,
      fill = "cornflowerblue",
      color = "navy",
      size = 3,
      alpha = alpha
    ) +
    geom_smooth(
      method = "lm",
      formula = y ~ x,
      se = FALSE,
      color = line_colour,
      linewidth = 1.5
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 80), ylim = range(one_sample$nitrate)) +
    labs(
      x = "Farmland within 1 km (%)",
      y = "Nitrate (mg/L)",
      title = sprintf("Slope = %.3f mg/L per %%", slope)
    )
}

# Shuffle farmland across wells 10,000 times, recalculating the slope each time
null_slopes <- replicate(1e4, {
  ols_slope(sample(one_sample$ag_pct), one_sample$nitrate)
})
# Two-sided: slopes at least as far from 0 as observed, in either direction
perm_pvalue <- mean(abs(null_slopes) >= abs(beta_1_hat))

# Resample wells with replacement 10,000 times, recalculating the slope each time
boot_slopes <- replicate(1e4, {
  resampled <- slice_sample(one_sample, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
  ols_slope(resampled$ag_pct, resampled$nitrate)
})
boot_ci <- quantile(boot_slopes, c(0.025, 0.975))

lm_pvalue <- coef(summary(one_sample_lm))["ag_pct", "Pr(>|t|)"]
lm_ci <- confint(one_sample_lm)["ag_pct", ]

slope_xlim <- c(-0.07, 0.09)
```

# Linear regression inference

## Learning objectives

- **Review inference**: hypothesis tests and confidence intervals
- Apply **hypothesis testing** to linear regression
- Apply **confidence intervals** to linear regression

## How today works

Each new method follows the same three steps:

1. **I do**: I explain it with slides
2. **We do**: we write the code together
3. **You do**: you fill in the blanks on a new problem

Live coding and exercises can be found [here](../labs/week5-monday-inference.qmd).

# Review inference

## Hypotheses

**Question**: _If_ there were no effect, _then_ how surprising is our sample?

- **Null hypothesis**, $H_0$: no effect. The skeptic's position.
- **Alternative hypothesis**, $H_A$: the effect we're looking for.

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.8em"}

| | $H_0$ | $H_A$ | Counts as "at least as extreme" |
|---|---|---|---|
| One-sided | $\beta_1 = 0$ | $\beta_1 < 0$ (or $> 0$) | One tail |
| Two-sided | $\beta_1 = 0$ | $\beta_1 \ne 0$ | Both tails |

:::

## Null distribution and p-value

The **null distribution** is what the statistic looks like across samples _if_ $H_0$ is true.

The **p-value** is the proportion of the null distribution at least as extreme as the observed statistic.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-align: center

observed_z <- 1.8
null_demo <- expand_grid(
  sides = c("One-sided: one tail", "Two-sided: both tails"),
  z = seq(-3.5, 3.5, by = 0.01)
) |>
  mutate(
    density = dnorm(z),
    extreme = if_else(
      str_starts(sides, "One"),
      z >= observed_z,
      abs(z) >= observed_z
    )
  )

ggplot(null_demo, aes(z, density)) +
  geom_area(
    aes(group = z > 0),
    filter(null_demo, extreme),
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_z, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = observed_z + 0.15,
    y = 0.35,
    label = "Observed",
    hjust = 0,
    size = 6
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~sides) +
  labs(x = "Statistic", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

Small p-value (< 0.05): the sample would be surprising under $H_0$, so we **reject** $H_0$.

## Two ways to get a null distribution

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Randomization: permutation**

_Shuffle_ the predictor to break its link with the response. Recalculate the statistic. Repeat 1,000s of times.

:::

::: {.column}

**Mathematical model**

Given enough independent observations, the null distribution is approximately

$$
Normal(0, SE)
$$

where $SE$ is the **standard error** of the statistic.

:::

:::

## Confidence intervals

**Question**: _How big_ is the effect?

A **confidence interval** is a range of plausible values for the population parameter. It comes from the **sampling distribution**: what the statistic looks like across many samples from the population.

::: {.fragment}

"95% confident" means: if we repeated the procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the population parameter.

:::

## 95% of intervals contain $\beta_1$

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-align: center

many_cis <- map(1:50, \(i) {
  wells <- slice_sample(simulated_population, n = 30)
  ci <- confint(lm(nitrate ~ ag_pct, wells))["ag_pct", ]
  tibble(sample = i, lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(contains = lower <= beta_1 & upper >= beta_1)

ggplot(
  many_cis,
  aes(y = sample, xmin = lower, xmax = upper, color = contains)
) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = beta_1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(`TRUE` = "grey50", `FALSE` = "darkorange"),
    labels = c(`TRUE` = "Contains", `FALSE` = "Misses")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression("95% CI for " * beta[1]),
    y = "Sample",
    color = NULL,
    title = sprintf(
      "%d of 50 intervals contain the population slope (dashed)",
      sum(many_cis$contains)
    )
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Two ways to get a sampling distribution

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Randomization: bootstrap**

_Resample_ the sample with replacement, as a stand-in for the population. Recalculate the statistic. Repeat 1,000s of times.

95% CI: the middle 95% of the bootstrap distribution.

:::

::: {.column}

**Mathematical model**

The sampling distribution is approximately

$$
Normal(\hat \beta_1, SE)
$$

:::

:::

## What's the same, what's new

Linear regression inference is the inference you already know.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

**Same**

- $H_0$, $H_A$, null distributions, p-values
- Sampling distributions, standard errors, CIs

:::

::: {.column}

**New**

- The statistic is a coefficient, $\hat \beta_1$
- `lm()` does the mathematical model for you

:::

:::

# Hypothesis testing with linear regression

## Scenario: nitrate in drinking water wells

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Fertilizer and manure leach nitrate into groundwater. Many rural Central Valley communities drink from wells. Above 10 mg/L is a health risk, especially for infants.

:::

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

A water agency tests 30 wells.

- $x$: farmland within 1 km (%)
- $y$: nitrate (mg/L)
- $\beta_1$: nitrate change per % farmland

$$
\text{Nitrate} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Farmland} + \epsilon
$$

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.7
plot_wells(one_sample, alpha = 1) +
  labs(caption = "Simulated data")
```

:::

:::

## Is the slope different from 0?

The sample slope is $\hat \beta_1$ = `r round(beta_1_hat, 3)` mg/L per %. But sampling is random!

::: {.fragment}

$H_0$: $\beta_1 = 0$ (farmland has no relationship with nitrate)

$H_A$: $\beta_1 \ne 0$ (farmland has a relationship with nitrate)

:::

# P-value by permutation 

## I do: shuffle the predictor

If $H_0$ is true, farmland is unrelated to nitrate, so shuffling farmland across wells shouldn't matter.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
plot_wells(one_sample) +
  labs(subtitle = "Observed")
```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
one_shuffle <- mutate(one_sample, ag_pct = sample(ag_pct))
plot_wells(one_shuffle, line_colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(subtitle = "Farmland shuffled")
```

:::

:::

## I do: the null distribution

Shuffle 10,000 times. Each shuffle gives one slope from the null distribution.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

p_perm <- tibble(slope = null_slopes) |>
  mutate(extreme = abs(slope) >= abs(beta_1_hat)) |>
  ggplot(aes(slope)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(fill = extreme),
    binwidth = 0.004,
    boundary = 0,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = beta_1_hat, linewidth = 1, color = "firebrick") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = -beta_1_hat,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "firebrick"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "steelblue")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = slope_xlim) +
  labs(
    x = expression("Slope under " * H[0]),
    y = "Count",
    title = sprintf("Permutation p = %.3f", perm_pvalue)
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_perm
```

Two-sided: count shuffles at least as far from 0 as `r round(beta_1_hat, 3)` in _either_ direction.

## I do: interpret the p-value

_If_ farmland had no relationship with nitrate, we would see a slope at least as far from 0 as `r round(beta_1_hat, 3)` mg/L per % in about `r scales::percent(perm_pvalue, accuracy = 0.1)` of samples.

::: {.fragment}

p < 0.05, so we reject $H_0$. The slope is _statistically significant_.

:::

# P-value by mathematical model

## I do: the null distribution, mathematically

Under $H_0$, the sampling distribution of $\hat \beta_1$ is approximately

$$
\hat \beta_1 \sim Normal(0, SE(\hat \beta_1))
$$

`lm()` estimates $SE(\hat \beta_1)$ from the residuals and the spread of the predictor. No shuffling needed.

## I do: read the coefficients table

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
one_sample_lm <- lm(nitrate ~ ag_pct, one_sample)
coef(summary(one_sample_lm))
```

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Estimate**: $\hat \beta_1$, the sample statistic
- **Std. Error**: $SE(\hat \beta_1)$, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution
- **t value**: Estimate / Std. Error, how many SEs $\hat \beta_1$ is from 0
- **Pr(>|t|)**: the **two-sided** p-value for $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$. For a one-sided $H_A$, divide by 2 (if $\hat \beta_1$ is in the direction of $H_A$).

:::

## I do: permutation vs mathematical model

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

normal_null <- tibble(
  slope = seq(slope_xlim[1], slope_xlim[2], length.out = 400),
  # Scale density to counts so it overlays the histogram
  count = dnorm(slope, 0, se_beta_1) * length(null_slopes) * 0.004
)
p_perm +
  geom_line(aes(slope, count), normal_null, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(
    title = sprintf(
      "Permutation p = %.3f   lm() p = %.3f",
      perm_pvalue,
      lm_pvalue
    )
  )
```

The normal curve (black) closely matches the permutation null distribution.

## I do: compare the p-values

| Method | p-value |
|---|:---:|
| Permutation | `r round(perm_pvalue, 3)` |
| `lm()`'s `Pr(>|t|)` | `r round(lm_pvalue, 3)` |

Same interpretation, same conclusion: reject $H_0$.

2. Compare it to the permutation p-value

# Confidence intervals with linear regression

## How much does nitrate increase?

We rejected $H_0$: farmland is related to nitrate. But _how much_ does nitrate increase per percentage point of farmland?

::: {.fragment}

**Question**: What's the interval we're confident contains the population slope, $\beta_1$?

:::

# Confidence interval by bootstrap

## I do: resample with replacement

Treat the sample as a stand-in for the population. Draw 30 wells _with replacement_ and refit.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
plot_wells(one_sample) +
  labs(subtitle = "Observed")
```

:::

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
one_resample <- slice_sample(one_sample, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
plot_wells(one_resample, line_colour = "darkorange", alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(subtitle = "Resampled (darker = drawn more)")
```

:::

:::

## I do: the bootstrap distribution {.nostretch}

Resample 10,000 times. The middle 95% is the 95% confidence interval.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: center

p_boot <- tibble(slope = boot_slopes) |>
  mutate(in_ci = between(slope, boot_ci[1], boot_ci[2])) |>
  ggplot(aes(slope)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(fill = in_ci),
    binwidth = 0.004,
    boundary = 0,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = beta_1_hat, linewidth = 1, color = "firebrick") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "darkorange")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = slope_xlim) +
  labs(
    x = "Slope (bootstrap distribution)",
    y = "Count",
    title = sprintf("Bootstrap 95%% CI: [%.3f, %.3f]", boot_ci[1], boot_ci[2])
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
p_boot
```

The bootstrap distribution is centered on $\hat \beta_1$ (red), not $H_0$.

## I do: interpret the confidence interval

We are 95% confident that nitrate increases by between `r round(boot_ci[1], 3)` and `r round(boot_ci[2], 3)` mg/L for each additional percentage point of farmland.

# Confidence interval by mathematical model

## I do: the sampling distribution, mathematically

The sampling distribution of $\hat \beta_1$ is approximately

$$
\hat \beta_1 \sim Normal(\beta_1, SE(\hat \beta_1))
$$

We don't know $\beta_1$, so center on $\hat \beta_1$. 

## I do: bootstrap vs mathematical model

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

normal_sampling <- tibble(
  slope = seq(slope_xlim[1], slope_xlim[2], length.out = 400),
  count = dnorm(slope, beta_1_hat, se_beta_1) * length(boot_slopes) * 0.004
)
p_boot +
  geom_line(aes(slope, count), normal_sampling, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lm_ci, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = sprintf(
      "Bootstrap [%.3f, %.3f]   confint() (dashed) [%.3f, %.3f]",
      boot_ci[1],
      boot_ci[2],
      lm_ci[1],
      lm_ci[2]
    )
  )
```

The standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution, `r round(sd(boot_slopes), 4)`, approximates the standard error, `r round(se_beta_1, 4)`.

## I do: let `confint()` do it

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: small-output
confint(one_sample_lm)
```

:::

| Method | 95% CI |
|---|:---:|
| Bootstrap | [`r round(boot_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(boot_ci[2], 3)`] |
| `confint()` | [`r round(lm_ci[1], 3)`, `r round(lm_ci[2], 3)`] |

Back to the lab, **Part 4**, _We do_.

1. Compare the bootstrap CI to `confint()`
2. Compare the bootstrap standard deviation to `Std. Error`

# Recap

## Four tools, two questions

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

| | Randomization | Mathematical model |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Is there an effect?** | Permutation: shuffle $x$, refit | `Pr(>|t|)` in `summary()` |
| **How big is it?** | Bootstrap: resample rows, refit | `confint()` |

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.8em"}

- Hypothesis tests center on $H_0$; confidence intervals center on $\hat \beta_1$
- Both mathematical tools rely on the **standard error**, `Std. Error` in `summary()`
- When the model's assumptions hold, randomization and mathematical models agree

:::
